turns.prompt_text: Where did the story behind iron lung come from?
turns.response_html:
The story of the iron lung—both the medical machine and the survival stories associated with it—is rooted in one of the most terrifying health crises of the 20th century: the global polio epidemics.

Here is how the idea was born, how it worked, and how it came to define an era.

The Invention: A Solution for "Forgotten" Muscles

In the early 1900s, poliomyelitis (polio) outbreaks routinely paralyzed children and adults. The most lethal form was bulbar or spinal polio, which paralyzed the diaphragm and intercostal muscles. Patients literally grew too tired to breathe and suffocated.

In 1928, an industrial hygienist at Harvard named Philip Drinker, along with medical resident Louis Agassiz Shaw, changed this. Drinker was actually investigating methods to resuscitate victims of gas poisoning and electric shock when he visited a children's hospital and saw room after room of children dying of respiratory failure from polio.

Determined to find a mechanical solution, he engineered the first tank respirator using relatively simple materials: a large sheet-metal cylinder, two domestic vacuum cleaners to control air pressure, and an automotive gear system to alternate the pump.

How the Physics Worked

The iron lung relied on negative pressure ventilation.

  1. The patient's body was sealed inside the airtight iron cylinder, with only their head protruding through a tight rubber collar.
  2. An external pump periodically sucked air out of the tank, creating a partial vacuum.
  3. This drop in external pressure forced the patient's chest chamber to expand, drawing fresh air into their nose and mouth (inhalation).
  4. The pump then allowed air back into the tank, increasing the pressure around the body, forcing the chest to contract and push the air out (exhalation).

The machine debuted at Boston Children’s Hospital in October 1928, successfully saving the life of an 8-year-old girl suffering from respiratory failure.

The Polio Wards of the 1940s and 50s

As epidemics intensified across the mid-20th century, hospital wards filled with rows of these massive mechanical cylinders, creating a surreal, industrial atmosphere defined by the rhythmic whoosh-click sound of alternating air bellows.

For many patients, the iron lung was a temporary bridge. Their bodies used the machine for a few weeks or months until their immune systems fought off the acute viral attack, their muscles recovered, and they could breathe independently again.

However, for a small percentage of patients, the damage to the motor neurons regulating respiration was permanent.

The Human Stories of Lifelong Survival

When Jonas Salk’s vaccine arrived in 1953 and Albert Sabin's oral vaccine followed, polio was rapidly eradicated in the developed world. Iron lungs quickly became obsolete, replaced by modern positive-pressure ventilators that push air directly into the airway via intubation or tracheostomy tubes.

Yet, a handful of individuals chose to stay in their iron lungs for the rest of their lives. They found the negative-pressure tanks less invasive and more comfortable than having tubes inserted into their throats. Two people became globally famous for living out their lives inside these machines:

  • Paul Alexander ("Polio Paul"): Contracted polio in Texas in 1952 at age 6. He spent over 70 years inside an iron lung. Defying his physical limitations, he learned "glossopharyngeal breathing" (gulping air into his lungs to leave the machine for a few hours at a time), went to college, earned a law degree, practiced law using a modified wheelchair, and wrote a memoir using a plastic rod held in his mouth to type. He passed away in early 2024.
  • Martha Lillard: Another lifelong user who contracted polio in 1953. As the years went on, a major challenge for people like Lillard and Alexander was finding replacement parts. Because companies stopped manufacturing the machines decades ago, they relied on independent mechanics, specialized hobbyists, and salvaged parts from old hospital basements to keep their lifesaving machinery running.

The story behind the iron lung is ultimately a transition from a frantic, mechanical scramble to beat a terrifying virus to an iconic symbol of human resilience and early biomedical engineering.

turns.response_html:
Yes, the connection is absolutely there, though it’s a brilliant bit of thematic wordplay!

Markiplier’s feature film Iron Lung is directly adapted from a massively popular indie horror video game of the same name, created by developer David Szymanski.

Why is it called "Iron Lung"?

In the story, the title doesn't refer to the medical device, but to a rusty, claustrophobic, one-man submarine officially designated as the SM-13.

However, the naming is highly intentional. The game's developer chose the nickname "Iron Lung" precisely because of the thematic parallels to the historical medical tank:

  • Total Enclosure: Just like the medical device, once you are inside, you are completely sealed in. In the movie's lore, the submarine's hatch is literally welded shut from the outside before it is dropped into the depths.
  • The Only Line to Life: The machine is the only thing keeping the occupant alive in an incredibly hostile environment, mechanically controlling their oxygen supply while keeping crushing external pressure at bay.

Where Did the Story Come From?

The origin of Iron Lung is a fascinating mix of a real-life vacation, cosmic horror, and classic low-visibility tension.

1. The Real-Life Inspiration: Loch Ness

David Szymanski originally got the idea for the core gameplay mechanic while visiting a Loch Ness museum in Scotland with his wife. He became fascinated by how researchers use sonar, ultrasound, and underwater cameras to try and map dark, murky waters where the human eye can't see.

He realized that forcing a player to navigate a submarine through tight spaces without a window—relying entirely on an old, slow, low-quality digital camera to see what is outside—would create an incredibly tense horror experience.

2. The Wild Sci-Fi Lore

Szymanski built a deeply unsettling cosmic horror universe around that concept, which Markiplier expanded into the two-hour film:

  • The Quiet Rapture: The story takes place in a dystopian future where every single star and habitable planet in the universe suddenly and inexplicably vanished into thin air. The only surviving humans are those who happened to be on space stations or spaceships at the time.
  • An Ocean of Blood: Desperate for resources to survive in the dying universe, the remaining human factions discover a desolate moon that has mysteriously formed an entire ocean of liquid human blood.
  • The Mission: The main character is a convict who is promised freedom if they pilot the tiny, windowless submarine down into the trenches of the blood ocean to photograph resources and anomalies.

The horror of the movie relies heavily on that absolute isolation. You are trapped in a tiny metal tube, blind to the outside world except for the grainy, delayed photos you take, knowing that something massive is shifting out there in the dark fluid.

turns.response_html:
You nailed it on both counts. David Szymanski is a seasoned indie horror veteran, and the narrative DNA of Iron Lung is a direct mashup of classic sci-fi tropes, existential dread, and psychological thrillers.

The Creator’s Horror Background

Before Iron Lung blew up, Szymanski was already highly respected in the indie gaming space. He is best known for creating DUSK, a massively successful retro-style shooter heavily inspired by 90s dark fantasy and horror classics like Quake and Blood.

He specializes in highly atmospheric, lo-fi aesthetic games (often using pixelated, retro graphics) that make environments feel inherently grimy, isolating, and unsettling. He also created short, bizarre horror micro-games like Fingerbones and Squirrel Stapler (which is exactly as weird and creepy as the title sounds).

The Story Mashup: Where the Elements Come From

The lore of Iron Lung didn't drop out of nowhere. It relies on a few distinct storytelling traditions:

1. Cosmic Horror & Lovecraftiana

The premise that every star and planet in the universe instantly vanished—known in the game as "The Quiet Rapture"—is pure cosmic horror. It taps directly into the Lovecraftian fear of an uncaring, incomprehensible universe where humanity is completely insignificant. The idea of an entire ocean made of human blood on a dead moon leans heavily into visceral, surreal body horror.

2. High-Concept 90s Sci-Fi

When Markiplier adapted the story for the feature film, he noted that his cinematic approach was heavily influenced by cult 90s sci-fi horror hits—particularly Event Horizon. That film features a rescue crew investigating a spaceship that vanished into another dimension and returned as a living, hellish entity. Iron Lung shares that exact same tone of dark, industrial sci-fi decay, where technology feels unsafe and sanity is actively slipping.

3. The "Submarine Thriller" Blueprint

Mechanically and structurally, the story borrows from classic submarine suspense films like Das Boot or The Hunt for Red October, where the primary enemy isn't necessarily a monster, but the ocean itself. The constant threat of hull breaches, mechanical failures, and the claustrophobia of being trapped in a metal tube under massive pressure are classic pillars of structural tension.

Szymanski simply took that classic military tension, stripped away the windows, drowned it in a sea of blood, and added a hint of an ancient cosmic nightmare waiting at the bottom.
